summary.text: Take \(n=7\). Since \(x\in\{3,4,6,10,15\}\), one has \(x\ge 3\), and the required ordering \(x\le y\le z\) forces \(x+y+z\ge 3x\ge 9\), contradicting \(x+y+z=7\).

full_proof.text:
We disprove the stated conjunction by showing that its strengthened “moreover” clause already fails at \(n=7\).

Recall that the conjecture says, in particular, that for every integer \(n>6\) there are positive integers \(x,y,z\) such that
\[
x\le y\le z,\qquad x+y+z=n,
\]
with
\[
x\in\{3,4,6,10,15\},
\]
and such that the six integers
\[
2x-1,\quad 2y-1,\quad 2z-1,\quad 2xy-1,\quad 2xz-1,\quad 2yz-1
\]
are all prime.

Take \(n=7\). Certainly \(7>6\), so if the conjecture were true, its strengthened clause would provide positive integers \(x,y,z\) satisfying all the conditions above and, in particular,
\[
x+y+z=7,\qquad x\le y\le z,\qquad x\in\{3,4,6,10,15\}.
\]

Membership in the displayed finite set can be analyzed explicitly. There are five cases:
\[
x=3,\quad x=4,\quad x=6,\quad x=10,\quad\text{or}\quad x=15.
\]
In every case, \(x\ge 3\). Since \(x\le y\) and \(y\le z\), we have both \(y\ge x\) and \(z\ge y\ge x\). Therefore
\[
x+y+z\ge x+x+x=3x.
\]
Because \(x\ge 3\), this implies
\[
x+y+z\ge 3\cdot 3=9.
\]
But the same alleged representation requires \(x+y+z=7\), which would give \(7\ge 9\), an impossibility.

Equivalently, one may see the contradiction separately in each of the five possible cases: if \(x=3\), orderedness forces the sum to be at least \(3+3+3=9\); if \(x=4\), it forces the sum to be at least \(12\); if \(x=6\), at least \(18\); if \(x=10\), at least \(30\); and if \(x=15\), at least \(45\). None can equal \(7\).

Thus \(7>6\) has no representation of the required strengthened form. This conclusion is reached before any primality conditions need to be considered: there is not even an ordered triple with the required sum and allowed value of \(x\). Hence the universal “moreover” assertion is false. Since that assertion is a conjunct of the full conjecture, the full conjecture is false, regardless of whether the separate claim \(a(n)>0\) for every \(n>5\) might hold.
